uses: Rosemary has long been tied to memory: folk custom carried it at weddings and funerals, and Culpeper wrote that it quickens a weak memory. In folk practice a warm tea of the leaves was taken after heavy meals for wind and a sluggish stomach, and rosemary baths and rubbing oils were used on stiff, chilly joints. A rinse of the dried herb was a traditional hair wash for dandruff. It was also burned in sickrooms to freshen the air, and it remains a favorite kitchen herb for meats, breads and vinegars.
taste: Pungent and aromatic, with a camphor-like note
energetics: Culpeper called rosemary hot and dry in the second degree
caution_pregnancy: Safety of medicinal rosemary during pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established, and the EMA does not recommend it then. Not enough is known; avoid medicinal amounts. The EMA's advice covers medicinal teas and baths, not seasoning food.
caution_medications: The EMA reports no known interactions. Few studies have looked, so if you take regular medicines, ask a pharmacist before using rosemary medicinally.
caution_conditions: If you have a blocked bile duct, gallstones, liver disease or another bile-duct problem, don't take rosemary by mouth without medical supervision. Medicinal use isn't recommended for children under 12. With high blood pressure, take care with full hot rosemary baths. See a doctor for a joint that is swollen, red or feverish, or for a sudden painful, hot or swollen leg.
caution_duration: If stomach symptoms last more than 2 weeks, or joint or circulation complaints more than 4 weeks, see a doctor or qualified practitioner.
caution_topical: Contact dermatitis (an allergic skin reaction) has been reported; how often isn't known. Don't put rosemary preparations on broken or irritated skin. Keep rosemary oil away from the eyes and the inside of the nose and mouth.
garden_harvest_timing: Snip the leafy upper shoot tips as needed through the year; the plant takes heavy pruning after it flowers.
garden_water: Dry to medium; needs good drainage and dies from overwatering
notes: Botanists moved rosemary into the sage genus, so older books call it Rosmarinus officinalis. An evergreen shrub that dislikes wet, humid sites and clay; it is slow from seed and easier from cuttings or layering. Bees, butterflies and hummingbirds visit the flowers. Culpeper placed it under the Sun and the sign of the Ram (Aries). Grieve records an old saying that a thriving rosemary bush showed who ruled the household.
